questions.q: Why does training an agent against real environments become especially costly at RL training's typical scale?
options: Real environments are always technically impossible to connect to an RL loop
RL training requires thousands to millions of rollouts, and running every one against a real system multiplies real API costs, rate limits, and latency by that same large factor
Real environments never have any API rate limits
Simulations are always slower than real environments
questions.explain: The large rollout volume needed for RL training means any per-call real-world cost, latency, or risk gets multiplied by that volume, which is the central reason simulations are often preferred for bulk training.

questions.q: What is the "sim-to-real gap" as described in this lesson?
options: The literal physical distance between a simulated server and a real one

The mismatch between behavior learned inside a simulation and what's actually required against the real system, arising because a simulation never perfectly reproduces real failure modes, quirks, or behaviors
A gap that only affects robotics applications, never LLM agents
The time delay between simulation and training completion
questions.explain: A policy can learn to exploit a simulation's specific characteristics, which don't transfer to the real environment's actual (and often messier) behavior, causing underperformance after deployment.

questions.q: What three mitigations does the lesson recommend when real-environment interaction during training is unavoidable?
options: Ignoring the risk entirely and running directly against production systems
Using sandboxed/staging accounts instead of production, enforcing hard rate and spending caps independent of the policy, and gating irreversible actions behind human or rule-based approval
Only using simulation and never interacting with any real system
Reducing the number of training rollouts to zero
questions.explain: These three safeguards — sandboxing, rate/spend limits, and approval gates for irreversible actions — are the lesson's recommended middle ground when a simulation can't fully substitute for real interaction.

questions.q: What does the lesson's "hybrid curriculum" recommend for sequencing simulation and real-environment training?
options: Train entirely in a real environment from the very first rollout

Train predominantly in simulation early (where mistakes are free and rollout volume can be huge), then mix in a smaller number of real, often sandboxed, episodes later to catch and correct sim-to-real gaps
Alternate randomly between simulation and reality with no particular order
Never use simulation at any point in training
questions.explain: The hybrid curriculum front-loads cheap simulated training and reserves real-environment interaction for later validation and correction, mirroring the staged approach to reward shaping from lesson 63.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize treating real-environment evaluation as the trustworthy signal even when most training leaned on simulation?
options: Because simulated evaluation is always more accurate than real evaluation

Because a policy's performance in simulation can be inflated by over-specializing to the simulation's specific quirks, so real-environment results are needed to confirm the improvement actually transfers
Because real-environment evaluation requires no safety precautions at all
Because simulations cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances
questions.explain: This connects directly to the sim-to-real gap: good simulated performance doesn't guarantee good real-world performance, so real-environment evaluation is needed to validate that training gains genuinely transferred.
